claims.text: Business activity organises resources to provide goods or services that satisfy wants and needs. A need is something essential for living, while a want is a particular way someone would like a need or desire satisfied. Producing something is not sufficient for commercial success: the offer must reach customers at a price and quality they accept. A private enterprise normally seeks enough revenue to cover costs and provide a return; other organisations may prioritise a service or social objective.

claims.text: Omuti Foods is an invented small bakery supplying bread to families in a Namibian town. The bakery combines ingredients, equipment and people to make bread available locally. Customers obtain food without baking it themselves, while sales give the bakery revenue with which to pay its costs. Revenue is not the same as profit: costs must be deducted. A shortage of customers or rising costs can prevent an otherwise useful business from surviving.

claims.text: A community includes customers, workers, nearby residents and other organisations. Businesses can respond by supplying needed goods and services, creating work, purchasing from local suppliers and supporting useful local projects. A response is stronger when the business first identifies a specific need rather than assuming that everyone wants the same thing. Community benefit and business benefit may coincide, but a useful service can still be costly to provide.

claims.text: Families near Omuti Foods need bread before the early bus leaves, and the bakery has an unused early shift. Opening earlier could make breakfast purchases more convenient and increase sales if enough families use the service. Hiring local workers can bring household income into the area. The bakery must compare the extra demand with wages, electricity and transport costs: a community response is more sustainable when it can be maintained without exhausting the business’s resources.

claims.text: The five basic activity types are primary, manufacturing, wholesale, retail and service. They describe what a business does, rather than its legal ownership. Primary activity extracts or obtains natural resources. Manufacturing changes materials into products. Wholesaling buys goods in bulk and supplies other businesses; retailing supplies final consumers. Service activity provides an activity, skill or assistance rather than principally transferring ownership of a physical product.

claims.text: An invented grower supplies grain, a mill processes it, and Omuti Foods makes bread for households. The grower’s activity is primary. Milling grain and making bread involve manufacturing. A distributor buying large consignments for shops is a wholesaler; a shop selling loaves to households is a retailer. A vehicle-repair workshop supporting deliveries supplies a service. One enterprise can carry out more than one activity, so classification should identify the particular operation being described.

claims.text: To distinguish activities, follow what happens to the resource or product and who receives the output. Extraction differs from transformation; selling to another business differs from selling to the final consumer. A service can support a physical product without itself being manufacturing. These distinctions prevent classifying an enterprise solely from its size, its name or the fact that it earns money.

claims.text: An invented fishing operation lands fish; a processor freezes packaged portions; a shop sells them to families. A firm buying cartons from the processor and reselling them to shops performs wholesaling. The ownership form could be the same at several stages without changing the activity performed.

claims.text: Government can provide services and infrastructure, regulate business activity, raise revenue and influence economic conditions. Public services may support business by improving skills, transport or health. Regulation can address harms that private decisions impose on others. Fiscal policy concerns government spending and taxation; monetary policy concerns monetary and credit conditions, including interest rates. The tools differ, and their effects depend on the situation rather than being guaranteed.

claims.text: In a hypothetical policy example, a road improvement shortens Omuti Foods’ delivery route while borrowing becomes more expensive. The road can reduce delivery delays and transport expense, helping the bakery reach customers. A higher borrowing cost can make a new oven less affordable, so expansion may be postponed. Government expenditure on the road is a fiscal action; the change in credit conditions belongs to monetary policy. Calling both tools taxation would hide the different mechanisms.

claims.text: Economic systems concern how resources are allocated and how production decisions are made. In a market model, private decisions and prices have a major coordinating role. In a planned model, central public decisions direct a substantial part of production and allocation. A mixed economy combines private enterprise with public ownership, provision and regulation. These are models: actual economies differ in the extent and form of intervention.

claims.text: An invented town has privately owned bakeries and publicly provided roads and schools. The town illustrates a mixed arrangement: private producers decide what bread to offer, while public provision supports the community. Market competition may encourage responsiveness and cost control, but people with little purchasing power may not obtain all the services they need. Planning can pursue collective priorities, but planners may lack detailed local information. A comparison should connect a feature to its consequence rather than label one system good in every situation.

claims.text: Specialisation means concentrating on a particular activity, product or skill. Division of labour is a form of specialisation in which production is split into tasks and workers concentrate on particular tasks. The ideas are related but operate at different scales: a business may specialise in bread, and its workers may divide mixing, shaping and baking between them.

evidence.locator: PDF p.8; objective OBJ-6144-1.1.07. Author's explanation of the cited syllabus demand, not a verbatim source quotation.

verification.method: Author draft; source-linked concepts and original examples await independent subject review.

claims.text: Omuti Foods produces bread, with different workers mixing dough, shaping loaves and operating an oven. The firm specialises in a narrow product range. Its workers’ separate tasks illustrate division of labour. Repetition can build skill and reduce time lost switching tasks, but the stages depend on one another. If the oven is unavailable, faster shaping alone does not produce finished loaves. Specialisation therefore needs coordination as well as individual skill.

claims.text: Specialisation can be considered between countries, between regions, between industries and between individual businesses. At each level a unit concentrates on activities suited to its resources or capabilities. A level describes the scale of concentration; it is not a rank in a management hierarchy. Different levels can exist at the same time.

evidence.locator: PDF p.8; objective OBJ-6144-1.1.08. Author's explanation of the cited syllabus demand, not a verbatim source quotation.

verification.method: Author draft; source-linked concepts and original examples await independent subject review.

claims.text: An invented coastal region concentrates on fishing, while a particular business concentrates on repairing fishing equipment. The region’s concentration is regional specialisation. The repair firm’s focus is specialisation between businesses. The examples do not identify a managing director or supervisor: those are management levels, not levels of specialisation. Concentration creates reasons to exchange with other regions or businesses for goods and services not produced locally.

evidence.locator: PDF p.8; objective OBJ-6144-1.1.08. Author's explanation of the cited syllabus demand, not a verbatim source quotation. Original illustrative reasoning/context.

verification.method: Author draft; source-linked concepts and original examples await independent subject review.

claims.text: Specialisation can improve skill through repetition, reduce time spent changing tasks and allow equipment to be used intensively. These gains may raise output or reduce unit costs if the stages are coordinated and demand supports the output. Limitations include repetitive work, dependence on other stages and a loss of flexibility. A specialised skill or product may become less useful when demand changes. Skills for cover can be developed through on-the-job or off-the-job training; the choice of training method is explained in Topic 3.5, while the point here is continuity between specialised tasks.

evidence.locator: PDF p.8; objective OBJ-6144-1.1.09. Author's explanation of the cited syllabus demand, not a verbatim source quotation.

verification.method: Author draft; source-linked concepts and original examples await independent subject review.

claims.text: Omuti Foods has steady orders for standard loaves but is considering accepting many individually decorated celebration breads. A task-based line suits repeated standard loaves because workers can practise a narrow activity and organise batches efficiently. It may be less suitable when orders differ substantially or one absent worker stops a stage. A sensible judgement is to specialise the repeated standard work while retaining flexible skills for varied orders. If most demand becomes individual orders, that balance should change.

claims.text: Trade is the buying and selling or exchange of goods and services. Specialisation and trade support each other: concentrating on some activities leaves other needs to be met through exchange, while access to a wider market can make specialisation worthwhile. Selling output can provide the income needed to buy inputs or other products. Trade still depends on reliable supply, demand and acceptable terms.

evidence.locator: PDF p.8; objective OBJ-6144-1.1.10. Author's explanation of the cited syllabus demand, not a verbatim source quotation.

verification.method: Author draft; source-linked concepts and original examples await independent subject review.

claims.text: Omuti Foods specialises in bread and purchases flour and repair services from other invented local suppliers. The bakery does not need to grow grain and repair every machine itself. It can sell bread and use revenue to buy those inputs and services. This allows attention to be focused on baking, but creates dependence on suppliers. If flour deliveries become unreliable, the benefits of concentration may be reduced. Trade is the exchange linking specialised activities; it is not another name for the specialisation itself.

claims.text: Stakeholders are groups or individuals with an interest in a business’s activities or outcomes. They include consumers, workers, managers, owners, finance providers and the wider community. A person can belong to more than one group: an employee may also buy the product or own part of the enterprise. Their interests should be identified from the business relationship, not from an unrelated category.

evidence.locator: PDF p.8; objective OBJ-6144-1.1.11. Author's explanation of the cited syllabus demand, not a verbatim source quotation.

verification.method: Author draft; source-linked concepts and original examples await independent subject review.

claims.text: Omuti Foods employs workers, sells to households and has borrowed money for equipment. Workers have an employment interest, households have a customer interest and the lender has a repayment interest. A customer is a stakeholder even without working inside the bakery. A production sector such as manufacturing is an activity classification, not a stakeholder group. Informal friendships among employees are workplace groups, which is another classification again.

claims.text: An objective is a result a person or group wants to achieve. Consumers may seek value and dependable quality; workers may seek pay, safety and security; managers may seek effective performance and career progress. Owners may seek profit and long-term survival. Finance providers may seek repayment or a return consistent with risk. The community may seek jobs and useful services without excessive disturbance. These objectives can overlap but do not necessarily have equal priority.

evidence.locator: PDF p.8; objective OBJ-6144-1.1.12. Author's explanation of the cited syllabus demand, not a verbatim source quotation.

verification.method: Author draft; source-linked concepts and original examples await independent subject review.

claims.text: The owners of Omuti Foods are considering a later opening time, higher wages and a price increase. Higher pay may support workers but increase costs. A higher price could help cover those costs, yet reduce value for some customers and weaken demand. The lender is interested in whether the bakery can continue meeting repayments. Residents may care about delivery noise as well as employment. A decision should identify who gains or loses, rather than assume the owners’ objective represents every stakeholder.

evidence.locator: PDF p.8; objective OBJ-6144-1.1.12. Author's explanation of the cited syllabus demand, not a verbatim source quotation. Original illustrative reasoning/context.

verification.method: Author draft; source-linked concepts and original examples await independent subject review.

claims.text: Objectives conflict when pursuing one makes another harder to achieve. Conflict can occur between groups or within one group’s priorities. Raising wages can reduce short-term profit if other conditions are unchanged; reducing prices may help customers but leave less money to cover costs. A conflict is not proof that cooperation is impossible: changes in productivity or a negotiated compromise may help several groups.

evidence.locator: PDF p.8; objective OBJ-6144-1.1.13. Author's explanation of the cited syllabus demand, not a verbatim source quotation.

verification.method: Author draft; source-linked concepts and original examples await independent subject review.

claims.text: Workers at Omuti Foods request higher pay while customers resist a price rise and the owners need to maintain cash for repairs. Paying more without extra revenue increases costs and can reduce the funds available for repairs. Passing the full increase to customers may reduce sales. A phased wage change combined with feasible waste reduction could ease the conflict, but the savings must be achievable. The explanation must connect each objective to a constraint rather than merely list that groups want different things.

evidence.locator: PDF p.8; objective OBJ-6144-1.1.13. Author's explanation of the cited syllabus demand, not a verbatim source quotation. Original illustrative reasoning/context.

claims.text: Business priorities can change with survival pressures, resources, demand and stakeholder concerns. A new enterprise may emphasise establishing customers; a business facing a cash shortage may prioritise paying immediate bills. Once stable, it may give more attention to expansion, product improvement or staff development. Changing priorities does not necessarily mean abandoning the longer-term objective: it may change the sequence in which objectives are pursued.

claims.text: Omuti Foods planned a larger shop, but a delivery vehicle now needs urgent repair. Reliable deliveries may become the immediate priority because existing sales depend on them. A stronger explanation identifies the changed circumstance and why it alters the relative urgency of the objectives.
